title: Visitors Flock to China's Sacred Wudang Mountains
paragraphs: In central China's Wudang Mountains, temples and palaces stand among the peaks. The range has been a sacred place in Taoism for centuries. Today, it draws pilgrims who come to pray, as well as visitors drawn by its history and mountain scenery.

Wudang had 14 million visitors in 2025, according to government figures. One of its most important sites is the Golden Hall, which stands atop Tianzhu, the highest of the range's 72 peaks. Although it was constructed like a wooden building, its parts are made of bronze. Inside is a statue of Zhenwu, a deity believed to protect Wudang.
According to legend, Zhenwu was once a prince who came to the mountains to practice Taoism and eventually became immortal.

Among those who came to pray to him was Liu Haiyan, who traveled several hundred kilometers from Hebei province with her daughter. She asked Zhenwu to bless China with favorable weather and prosperity. "Everyone comes here with a sincere heart," she told the Associated Press.

Elsewhere in Wudang, visitors pray for other things. Wang Xia, who came from Inner Mongolia, visited a temple linked to Zhenwu's legendary life as a prince. She prayed for her daughter's success at school and a bright future.

Wudang's oldest Taoist buildings date back to the 7th century, but the complex grew especially large during the Ming dynasty. In the early 1400s, Emperor Zhu Di ordered a major building campaign there. More than 60 historic buildings and sites survive today, and the complex became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1994.

Wudang is also home to a living community. Taoist priests and monks still care for its temples, and many local families have grown up alongside them. Cai Hongping, who lived near one temple as a child, remembers gathering medicinal herbs and practicing martial arts with the priests. Although food was scarce, she recalls the temples as places of kindness and joy.
"The entire mountain was my childhood," Cai said.
